scenes.visual: THE WORLD, kept for both chapters (16:9, dark navy background). COLOUR BY CLASS, same in every scene: round yellow seeds GOLD; round green GREEN; wrinkled yellow ORANGE; wrinkled green TEAL. Expected counts are WHITE dashed 'ghost' lines; probabilities are WHITE text on branches; anything made by chance in a simulation is drawn in pale GREY first and takes its class colour when it settles. Chromosomes are BLUE rods. Numbers and fractions always appear on screen as text, never only spoken. Title card 'A Ratio Predicts a Spread' fades in, centred, over four faint seed silhouettes (round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow, wrinkled green) drifting slowly behind it.

scenes.tts: Why did none of Mendel's counts match his ratio? He crossed peas that differed in seed shape and seed colour. Then he counted the seeds from the hybrids.
scenes.caption: Why did none of Mendel's counts match his ratio? He crossed peas that differed in seed shape and seed colour. Then he counted the seeds from the hybrids.
scenes.visual: Title fades. Seeds pour from the top into four piles that grow into four vertical bars in the class colours, left to right GOLD, GREEN, ORANGE, TEAL, each labelled with its seed cartoon (round yellow, round green, wrinkled yellow, wrinkled green). Counter at top right ticks up to '556 seeds'. Final bar labels: 315, 108, 101, 32.
scenes.narration: Why did none of Mendel's counts match his ratio? He crossed peas that differed in seed shape and seed colour. Then he counted the seeds from the hybrids.

scenes.tts: His ratio predicts how the seeds should split into four kinds. Not one of his four piles matched its prediction. Was the ratio wrong?
scenes.caption: His ratio predicts how the seeds should split into four kinds. Not one of his four piles matched its prediction. Was the ratio wrong?
scenes.visual: '9 : 3 : 3 : 1' appears above the bars. A WHITE dashed ghost line drops onto each bar at its expected height, labelled 312.75, 104.25, 104.25, 34.75. Each small gap between bar top and ghost line flashes once. On 'Was the ratio wrong?' a white question mark appears above the bars.
scenes.narration: His ratio predicts how the seeds should split into four kinds. Not one of his four piles matched its prediction. Was the ratio wrong?

scenes.tts: Start with one seed. It began as an egg and a pollen grain. Each carried one version of each gene, picked by chance. So every seed is a fresh draw from the same odds. For seed shape alone, round comes up three times in four.
scenes.visual: Camera pushes into the GOLD bar and pulls out a single round seed. It splits into a cartoon egg (left) and pollen grain (right), each carrying two small gene tags: shape (R or r) and colour (Y or y). A coin-flip spin animates on each tag. Then a single fork appears for shape: upper branch 'round 3/4', lower branch 'wrinkled 1/4', in WHITE text.
scenes.narration: Start with one seed. It began as an egg and a pollen grain. Each carried one version of each gene, picked by chance. So every seed is a fresh draw from the same odds. For seed shape alone, round comes up three times in four.

scenes.tts: Now add seed colour as a second fork. To be round and yellow, a seed must take both branches. So follow the path, and multiply the chances along it.
scenes.visual: Each shape branch forks again: 'yellow 3/4' and 'green 1/4'. The path round then yellow glows GOLD; on screen beside its tip: '3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16'. The other three tips fill in: round green 3/16 (GREEN), wrinkled yellow 3/16 (ORANGE), wrinkled green 1/16 (TEAL). Small label 'schematic: two unlinked genes'.
scenes.narration: Now add seed colour as a second fork. To be round and yellow, a seed must take both branches. So follow the path, and multiply the chances along it.

scenes.tts: Some questions count more than one path. A seed with exactly one recessive trait could be round and green, or wrinkled and yellow. No seed can be both, so add those paths.
scenes.visual: The GREEN tip and the ORANGE tip both glow and their paths brighten. A bracket joins them with '3/16 + 3/16 = 6/16' on screen. The GOLD and TEAL paths dim to grey while this plays.
scenes.narration: Some questions count more than one path. A seed with exactly one recessive trait could be round and green, or wrinkled and yellow. No seed can be both, so add those paths.

scenes.tts: So the word and means multiply along a path. The word or means add the paths. Those two rules build the whole ratio.
scenes.caption: So the word 'and' means multiply along a path. The word 'or' means add the paths. Those two rules build the whole ratio.
scenes.visual: Two labels slide in at the bottom: 'AND: multiply along a path' and 'OR: add the paths'. The four tips 9/16, 3/16, 3/16, 1/16 lift off the tree and line up as '9 : 3 : 3 : 1'.
scenes.narration: So the word 'and' means multiply along a path. The word 'or' means add the paths. Those two rules build the whole ratio.

scenes.tts: But a ratio gives chances, not exact counts. Apply it to Mendel's total, and the round yellow pile comes out with part of a seed. You cannot grow three quarters of a seed. So a ratio cannot give the exact pile.
scenes.visual: Cut back to the four bars. On screen: '556 × 9/16 = 312.75'. A seed cartoon appears beside it, three quarters solid and one quarter outlined; the outlined quarter fades away. Label: 'chances, not a count'.
scenes.narration: But a ratio gives chances, not exact counts. Apply it to Mendel's total, and the round yellow pile comes out with part of a seed. You cannot grow three quarters of a seed. So a ratio cannot give the exact pile.

scenes.tts: So let chance grow the cross. A computer replays it with the same number of seeds, and the ratio exactly true. How far from the lines will the runs land?
scenes.caption: So let chance grow the cross. A computer replays it with the same number of seeds, and the ratio exactly true. How far from the lines will the runs land?
scenes.visual: The real bars fade to outlines; the WHITE ghost lines stay. A label 'simulation: 9:3:3:1 true, 556 seeds' appears top left. One simulated run fills the four bars in pale GREY, settling into class colours. On the question, a card appears: 'How far from the lines will the runs land?'
scenes.narration: So let chance grow the cross. A computer replays it with the same number of seeds, and the ratio exactly true. How far from the lines will the runs land?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. The question card stays. The single simulated run holds still beside the ghost lines; a small 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: No run can sit exactly on a line, since the lines fall at fractions of a seed. Each run lands a little high in one class and a little low in another, by its own amounts. Now drop in Mendel's real counts. They sit among the chance runs. His misses are well within what chance makes.
scenes.visual: Card dissolves. Twelve simulated runs replay in quick succession (about 0.5 s each, computed from a real multinomial draw with n = 556 and p = 9/16, 3/16, 3/16, 1/16); bar tops jiggle above and below the ghost lines and leave faint GREY tick marks, building a small cloud of ticks around each line. On 'Mendel's real counts', his bar tops (315, 108, 101, 32) drop in as bright WHITE ticks, inside each cloud.
scenes.narration: No run can sit exactly on a line, since the lines fall at fractions of a seed. Each run lands a little high in one class and a little low in another, by its own amounts. Now drop in Mendel's real counts. They sit among the chance runs. His misses are well within what chance makes.

scenes.tts: This works only when the steps are independent. Genes on different chromosomes pass on independently. Genes far apart on one chromosome behave almost as if unlinked. Genes close together tend to be inherited together. Then you cannot simply multiply their chances.
scenes.visual: Three panels. Left: two BLUE chromosome pairs, gene A on one, gene B on the other; a small two-gene tree beside them stays intact, labelled 'unlinked: multiply'. Middle: one BLUE chromosome with A and B far apart and a crossover point between them; its tree also stays intact, labelled 'far apart: almost unlinked'. Right: one BLUE chromosome with A and B side by side, a bracket 'inherited together'; the tree beside it has its branches tied with a knot and a red cross over '×', labelled 'linked: do not multiply'.
scenes.narration: This works only when the steps are independent. Genes on different chromosomes pass on independently. Genes far apart on one chromosome behave almost as if unlinked. Genes close together tend to be inherited together. Then you cannot simply multiply their chances.

scenes.tts: Here is the idea. A cross predicts probabilities. Multiply along a path, and add the paths that count. And a probability predicts a spread of counts, not one exact count.
scenes.visual: Back to the four ghost lines with their clouds of grey ticks. The words appear one line at a time on the left: 'A cross predicts probabilities.' 'Multiply along a path; add the paths.' 'A probability predicts a spread of counts.' Each cloud of ticks brightens slightly as the last line lands.
scenes.narration: Here is the idea. A cross predicts probabilities. Multiply along a path, and add the paths that count. And a probability predicts a spread of counts, not one exact count.

scenes.tts: So the real question is not whether counts match. It is how far a count can stray before chance becomes a poor explanation. That is chapter two.
scenes.caption: So the real question is not whether counts match. It is how far a count can stray before chance becomes a poor explanation. That is chapter 2.
scenes.visual: Camera pushes toward the edge of the GOLD cloud of ticks. A WHITE question mark appears just beyond its outermost tick, with the label 'how far is too far?'.
scenes.narration: So the real question is not whether counts match. It is how far a count can stray before chance becomes a poor explanation. That is chapter 2.

scenes.visual: End card over the dimmed world, large white text, centred: 'A ratio predicts a spread of counts, not one count.'
